title: Getting Set Up
exercise: Choose your start date and your daily reading spot. Write one honest sentence each for money, body, and stress.
description: For the next 21 days you'll work on three areas of your life: money, body, and stress. One small action a day. Today you just write down where you are.
hardDay: Just pick the start date.

title: Name Your Yo-Yo
exercise: Write down one area where you've been living on the yo-yo, and your honest baseline in that area right now. Don't judge it. Just name it.
description: The yo-yo: you push, you crash, you promise to restart. You can't bend a baseline you haven't named.
hardDay: Just name the area. Fill in the number tomorrow.

title: Your Peace of Mind Number
exercise: Add up one month of essentials: housing, food, utilities, getting to work, insurance, minimum payments. That's your Peace of Mind number. Then write down your first marker: $500 (or a smaller amount if that fits your situation better).
description: Your Peace of Mind Account is a separate savings account with one job: turning the next surprise bill from an emergency into an expense.
hardDay: Write down just your monthly housing cost. Finish the list tomorrow.

title: Your Body's Baseline
exercise: Start tracking three things for the next 7 days: movement (steps or minutes), what you eat at one meal each day, and sleep quality from 1 to 10. Just observe.
description: This week isn't about changing anything. It's about seeing what an ordinary week looks like.
hardDay: Just rate last night's sleep from 1 to 10.

title: Your Stress Blueprint
exercise: Do the 4x4x4x4 breath once. Then start your stress blueprint: what triggered stress, how your body responded, and how you recovered. Three entries over the next three days.
description: Stress has a pattern: a trigger, a response in your body, and a recovery (or not). Once you can see the pattern, you can work with it.
hardDay: Just do the breath once. Four rounds.

title: The Three-Pillar Snapshot
exercise: Write your three-pillar snapshot, one sentence each, with numbers. Example: 'I need $3,500 a month to cover essentials. I'm moving about 4,000 steps a day. Monday mornings are my biggest stress trigger.' Then draw at least one arrow connecting two of them.
description: Money stress can show up as tension in your body. Poor sleep can show up in your spending. It's one life, not three separate projects.
hardDay: Write just one of the three sentences.

title: Look Back at the Week
exercise: Write down three things you noticed about your baselines this week. A surprise, a pattern, or just a clearer number than before.
description: Reflection isn't journaling for its own sake. The pause is where you make sense of what you've been doing. Without it, a week of tracking is just a pile of numbers.
hardDay: Write down one.

title: Pick Your Anchor
exercise: Choose one number from this week to be your anchor: your Peace of Mind number, your daily steps, or your top stress trigger. Write it somewhere you'll see it every day. Open your Peace of Mind Account if you've decided to.
description: One number you see every day is a simple reminder of what you're working on.
hardDay: Write your anchor number on a sticky note. Stick it anywhere.

title: Where the Money Goes
exercise: Sort your last 30 days of spending into Essentials, Comfort, and Leaks. Pick one leak to plug this week, and move that amount into your Peace of Mind Account. Then look at the list once more and ask: if a stranger saw only this, what would they say my priorities are?
description: Spending can run on autopilot. Leaks are a good place to start, because plugging them costs you nothing you were enjoying. The last question is adapted from what author James Clear calls the alien test: if someone saw only your actions, and couldn't hear your explanations, what would they say your priorities are?
hardDay: Find one subscription you don't use and cancel it.

title: Just a Little More
exercise: Take your movement baseline from last week and add 5 to 10 percent. If you averaged 4,000 steps, aim for 4,200 to 4,400. Write down your one simple action and start it today.
description: A small change is easier to fit into an ordinary week. You can add a little more later.
hardDay: Walk for two extra minutes. That counts.

title: Stress Is Data
exercise: Pick one trigger from your blueprint. Write the trigger, your body's response, and what you needed in that moment. Do the 4x4x4x4 breath at least once.
description: A stress reaction isn't a character flaw. It's something you can notice and learn from.
hardDay: Do the breath once. Name the trigger in one word.

title: Find Your Biggest Opportunity
exercise: Reread your Day 5 snapshot. In each pillar, circle the biggest opportunity for about a 15 percent improvement.
description: Fifteen percent is noticeable but not an overhaul. Adjust it down if it feels like too much. Next week you'll turn these into moves.
hardDay: Circle one opportunity in one pillar.

title: Keep Score, Simply
exercise: Set up your three-column tracker (money, body, stress) and fill in today's row. Paper, your phone's notes, or the check-in in this app all work.
description: You don't need a fancy system. You need to be able to see, at a glance, whether you did the thing.
hardDay: Put a check mark on today's date on a calendar if you did your one simple action.

title: What You Wish You'd Known
exercise: Write down the one thing you wish you'd had clarity on earlier. Then write one simple way to keep it visible from now on.
description: The thing you wish you'd known sooner is the thing worth building a system around.
hardDay: Just write the one thing.

title: Halfway
exercise: Write down three changes you've noticed since Day 1, and the one thing you want to nail in the last week.
description: Two weeks in, the changes may be small. Writing them down gives you something concrete to look back on, and it points your last week at what matters most.
hardDay: Write one change.

title: Your Next Move, Part 1: Line Them Up
exercise: Find one place where two pillars are working against each other. Write down one small fix, and start it today.
description: When one pillar undercuts another, fixing the connection can help in more than one area.
hardDay: Just name the two pillars that fight the most.

title: Your Next Move, Part 2: Your 15 Percent Moves
exercise: Write down your three 15 percent moves, one per pillar: a leak or comfort expense to trim, a movement or eating adjustment, a change in how you respond to stress. Choose one and start it today.
description: Each move is specific enough that someone could tell whether you did it, and small enough to do in a bad week.
hardDay: Write down one move and start it.

title: Your Next Move, Part 3: Lock It In
exercise: For the move you started, write down and set up one thing that makes it happen without relying on motivation. An automatic transfer, a calendar block, shoes by the door.
description: Motivation comes and goes. Something set up ahead of time keeps working on the days you don't feel like it.
hardDay: Set up one small thing ahead of time for the move you chose, like a $5 weekly automatic transfer or your shoes by the door.

title: Hook It to Something You Already Do
exercise: Choose one daily routine (your morning coffee, brushing your teeth, getting into bed) and attach your new move to it. Write down the routine and the action.
description: A routine you already do every day is a reliable reminder. Many writers on habits have described this idea; it isn't original to this app.
hardDay: Attach one round of breathing to your morning coffee, or whatever you do first every day.

title: When You Slip
exercise: Write your reset plan in one paragraph. What's your smallest restart in each pillar? When do you restart? (The very next chance.) What will you ask? ("What got in the way?" not "What's wrong with me?")
description: You're going to slip. That's information, not failure. A 2010 University College London study found that missing one chance to do a new behavior did not meaningfully set back how the habit formed. What matters is the restart.
hardDay: Write just your smallest restart for each pillar.

title: Your One Page
exercise: Fill in your one page. Money: my Peace of Mind number, today's balance, my automatic transfer, my next milestone, and my next-dollar step. Body: my movement baseline, my one simple action, my 15 percent move. Stress: my most common trigger, my reset routine, my cue to use it. Anchors: when ___ happens, I ___. And one line for when I slip.
description: One page you can read in a minute. An honest page with a few blanks is more useful than a complete one full of guesses. Your next-dollar step is where your next available dollar goes. The Roadmap order: once your separate Peace of Mind Account reaches $1,000, enough to get the full company match if your plan offers one, then high-interest debt if you have any, then the rest of your Peace of Mind number.
hardDay: Fill in just the three "My ... is" lines you know best.

title: What Comes Next
exercise: Reread your Day 0 sentences. Write three new ones about where you are today in money, body, and stress. Set calendar reminders for 30, 60, and 90 days from now.
description: The 21 days end here. Your 30, 60, and 90-day reminders give you three chances to look again and adjust. Starting tomorrow, this app switches to Keep Your Margin: a short daily check-in and a five-minute weekly check.
hardDay: Set just the 30-day reminder.
